nameStory: The Coastal Swamp Amphipod gets its name from its preferred habitat along New England's coastal wetlands, where saltwater meets fresh in marshy areas. The scientific name 'Sicifera' means 'dagger-bearer,' likely referring to the sharp-pointed structures on its body, while 'chamberlaini' honors an early researcher who studied these tiny crustaceans.
description: This is a tiny, shrimp-like creature that lives in the brackish waters of coastal swamps and marshes. About the size of a grain of rice (3-8mm long), it has a flattened, curved body that's pale translucent white to light brown. Like all amphipods, it swims on its side and has a distinctly hunched appearance. You'll need a magnifying glass or good eyes to spot these little crustaceans darting through shallow marsh water.

idTips.label: Body shape and swimming
idTips.description: Swims on its side with a characteristic comma-shaped, laterally flattened body that feels firm but flexible when gently handled

idTips.label: Size and color
idTips.description: Tiny rice grain-sized body (3-8mm) that's translucent white to pale brown, often with a slightly cloudy appearance

idTips.label: Antennae
idTips.description: Two pairs of thread-like antennae that are constantly twitching and feeling around, often longer than the body

idTips.label: Movement pattern
idTips.description: Jerky, darting swimming motion through shallow water, often in quick bursts followed by brief pauses

idTips.label: Legs
idTips.description: Seven pairs of jointed legs visible under magnification, with the front pairs modified for grasping small food particles

habitat: Found in brackish coastal marshes, swamps, and tide pools where saltwater mixes with freshwater runoff throughout New England's coast. Look for them in shallow, vegetated areas with soft muddy bottoms, often among salt marsh grasses like cordgrass and pickleweed. They prefer areas with some protection from wave action but regular tidal influence.

seasonality.spring: Most active as temperatures warm, often found in larger numbers in shallow marsh pools. Breeding activity increases, so you may spot mating pairs.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period with highest populations visible. Best time for observation in warm, shallow tide pools during low tide periods.
seasonality.fall: Still active but beginning to move to deeper water. Numbers may appear to decline in shallow observation areas.
seasonality.winter: Much less visible as they retreat to deeper, more protected waters. May be found under ice in unfrozen marsh channels.

funFact: Despite being only the size of a rice grain, these amphipods are incredibly tough survivors that can live in water ranging from nearly fresh to almost as salty as the ocean - a salinity tolerance that would kill most other small freshwater creatures instantly.
confusionNotes: Often confused with tiny mysid shrimp or water fleas, but amphipods swim on their side (not upright) and have a distinctly flattened, comma-shaped profile. Remember: 'Amphipods on their side, shrimp swim upright with pride.'
contextualKnowledge: The extremely low observation count (only 7 recorded) doesn't mean these are rare - it reflects how rarely people look for or identify these tiny marsh creatures. Most beachgoers and even many naturalists overlook these abundant but inconspicuous animals.
compareHints: As the only Sicifera species in New England, it's most similar to other crangonyctid amphipods in coastal areas. However, most related species prefer purely freshwater environments, while S. chamberlaini specifically thrives in the brackish mixing zones. Its tolerance for saltwater and coastal marsh habitat sets it apart from its freshwater cousins.
